rfm_tuples.R: Based on that evaluation, our chief executive officer and our principal financial officer concluded that these disclosure controls and procedures were not effective as of April 27, 2024 due to the identified material weaknesses... Management identified a material weakness in our internal financial reporting controls over the review of the Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows, including operating lease disclosures and presentation at January 27, 2024, October 28, 2023, July 29, 2023, April 29, 2023, January 28, 2023, October 29, 2022 and July 30, 2022.
rfm_tuples.f: Verify scope of restated/affected periods and remediation status via subsequent 10-Q. Cross-check whether prior periods were restated and whether remediation is timely.
rfm_tuples.M_source: self_text + claim_evolution (FY2024 10-K vs Q1 FY2025 10-Q filed 2024-09-05)
rfm_tuples.M_value: Material weakness covers SEVEN prior interim/annual periods (Q2 FY23 through Q3 FY24) — i.e., management previously certified those periods as effective and is now reversing that conclusion. RSM US LLP audit report describes the MW: 'do not include correct differences between classifications within the statement of cash flows and the presentation of right-of-use assets obtained in exchange for lease liabilities as supplemental non-cash items.' Per FY2024 10-K Note 13, a Revision was made: cash from ops, investing, financing restated by ($10.0M)/($1.8M)/($11.6M) for prior periods; deemed not material. Q1 FY2025 10-Q (filed 2024-09-05) declares MW remediated within one quarter via 'enhanced communication... additional quarter-end reviews.' Q3 FY2025 10-Q (2025-03-06) reaffirms effective.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Material weakness in a defensive-stable, low-leverage beverage company is unusual. Scope spans ~7 quarters and forced cash-flow statement revisions across multiple years. Remediation in one quarter (already by Q1 FY25) is unusually fast — could be genuine (the fix is narrow: ROU asset cash-flow classification) or could indicate the new auditor's pressure rather than a deep-rooted control gap. Honest disclosure (no concealment), but a forensic red flag for a 'boring' name.

rfm_tuples.R: /s/ RSM US LLP We have served as the Company's auditor since 2006. Fort Lauderdale, Florida June 26, 2024.
rfm_tuples.f: auditor_change_tracker — verify no Item 4.01 8-K disclosure of resignation/dismissal within 6-12 months of MW disclosure. Mode B: did the MW trigger an auditor change?
rfm_tuples.M_value: 8-K filed 2024-11-06 (just over 4 months after the FY2024 10-K) discloses: 'On October 31, 2024, the Audit Committee approved the appointment of Grant Thornton LLP... [and] dismissed RSM US LLP.' RSM had served since 2006 (18-year tenure). 8-K asserts 'no disagreements (as defined in Item 304(a)(1)(iv))' and that audit reports were not qualified. However the dismissal occurred immediately after RSM signed the FY2024 10-K disclosing the multi-period material weakness — and the dismissal is mid-fiscal-year ('beginning with the Company's second fiscal quarter').
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B catch — the MW disclosure and the 18-year-tenure auditor's dismissal four months later are very likely related. The company frames it as 'solicited proposals from several accounting firms,' but the timing (mid-year switch, immediately post-MW) is suggestive that either RSM declined to continue or management wanted a fresh audit eye. Not a SEVERE flag because (a) RSM did sign the FY24 financials, (b) GT is a national firm (lateral move, not a downgrade), (c) no Item 304 disagreements reported. Still, an 18-year auditor leaving mid-year right after a material weakness is the textbook 'cluster of related-party / governance / control disclosures' pattern.

rfm_tuples.R: Pursuant to a management agreement, we incurred fees to Corporate Management Advisors, Inc. (CMA) of $11.9 million and $11.7 million for Fiscal 2024 and Fiscal 2023, respectively... The Company is a party to a management agreement with Corporate Management Advisors, Inc. (CMA), a corporation owned by our Chairman and Chief Executive Officer. This agreement was originated in 1991... Under the terms of the agreement, CMA provides... senior corporate functions (including supervision of the Company's financial, legal, executive recruiting and financial-reporting functions)... CMA and the Company are joint owners of a corporate aircraft.
rfm_tuples.f: Cross-check related-party payment magnitude vs disclosure, verify whether CMA personnel include the CFO/principal financial officer (governance independence test). Mode B: derive whether financial-reporting function being run by Chairman's controlled entity (CMA) overlaps with the locus of the material weakness in cash-flow statement controls.
rfm_tuples.M_value: CMA is owned 100% by 88-year-old Chairman/CEO Nick A. Caporella and provides 'supervision of the Company's financial-reporting functions.' Both EVP-Finance (George Bracken, 78) and Chairman/CEO are 'provided' to the Company by CMA — i.e., the company's principal financial officer is not a direct employee of FIZZ but of the Chairman's privately-held management company. Management fee = 1% of consolidated net sales (uncapped formula); $11.9M in FY24 vs $11.7M / $11.4M prior. Joint aircraft ownership $1.1M/yr average operating costs. Year-end CMA payable: $3.0M / $2.9M (FY24/FY23). No incentive comp paid 1991-2024 per disclosure. Management agreement dates to 1991 and the original 'two public companies' rationale ceased in 1994 per the filing itself.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B: the company discloses CMA fees and the related-party relationship — that part is honest. But the IMPLICATION of CMA — that the principal financial officer reports to a Caporella-owned entity, not to an independent FIZZ board — is not highlighted in MD&A or risk factors. Combined with the multi-period material weakness in financial-reporting controls, the picture is: the function that failed (cash-flow statement classifications) is outsourced to the Chairman's controlled entity. The 1994 rationale is stale (acknowledged in the filing). $11.9M/yr is ~6.8% of operating income — not trivial.

rfm_tuples.R: At April 27, 2024 and April 29, 2023, no customer comprised more than 10% of trade receivables. No customer accounted for more than 10% of net sales during any of the last three fiscal years.
rfm_tuples.f: Verify against XBRL concentration disclosures (NumberOfMajorCustomers). Mode B: derive whether 'no >10%' is actually true vs strategically structured to skirt threshold.
rfm_tuples.M_value: XBRL inline tagging confirms NumberOfMajorCustomers = 0 for FY2022, FY2023, FY2024 for both SalesRevenueNetMember and AccountsReceivableMember concentration axes. Consistent across periods. MD&A does note retail customer base 'has been consolidating over many years resulting in fewer customers with increased buying power.'
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Customer concentration claim is internally consistent and XBRL-tagged. Honest disclosure of a benign metric. The forward-looking risk (retailer consolidation) is acknowledged in risk factors.

rfm_tuples.R: Our principal sources of liquidity are our existing cash and cash-equivalents, cash generated from operations and borrowing capacity available under our revolving credit facilities. At April 27, 2024, we had $327.0 million in cash and cash equivalents and maintained unsecured revolving credit facilities totaling $150 million, under which no borrowings were outstanding... On June 12, 2024, the Company's board of directors declared a special cash dividend of $3.25 per share.
rfm_tuples.f: Verify dividend magnitude vs cash position; check whether the $304M special dividend was within retained earnings/working capital and whether timing (post-MW disclosure) is unusual. Cross-check with Q1/Q2 FY2025 cash flow.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Special dividend $3.25/sh on 93.6M outstanding = $304.1M, paid July 24, 2024. FY24 cash position $327M (essentially the entire balance). This is the THIRD special dividend in 4 years ($280M Jan 2021, $279.9M Dec 2021, $304M Jul 2024 — together $864M to shareholders, ~93% of FY24 trailing operating cash flow plus accumulated cash). No debt outstanding. Working capital $398.9M at FY24-end, dropping post-dividend. Q3 FY25 10-Q shows cash still at meaningful balance — generated operating cash funded the gap. Subsidiary covenant compliance confirmed each period.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Liquidity claim is verified and consistent. The dividend is large but funded by accumulated cash, not debt. Mode B note: the $3.25 special dividend was DECLARED June 12, 2024 — 14 days BEFORE the FY24 10-K (June 26, 2024) was filed with its material-weakness disclosure. The 73%-owner Chairman captured ~74% (~$225M) of the special. Not a forensic red flag in isolation, but a pattern: equity-holder Chairman extracts cash before disclosure of governance weakness.

rfm_tuples.R: Net sales for Fiscal 2024 increased 1.6% to $1,191.7 million compared to $1,172.9 million for Fiscal 2023. The increase in sales resulted primarily from a 1.8% increase in average selling price per case, partially offset by a 0.2% decline in case volume. The volume decline primarily impacted Power+Brands, partially offset by an increase in carbonated soft drink brands.
rfm_tuples.f: Claim evolution — verify whether volume trends continued or accelerated post-fiscal-year-end. Power+Brands (LaCroix) volume decline is a key competitive signal for the sparkling-water franchise.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Q1 FY25 (3 mo to 7/27/2024): volume +0.7%, sales +1.6%. Q2 FY25 (3 mo to 10/26/2024): volume -4.6%, sales -3.0% — decrease 'impacted both Power+Brands and carbonated soft drink brands.' Q3 FY25 (3 mo to 1/25/2025): volume -3.4%, sales -1.1%. Nine months FY25: volume -2.3%, sales -0.7%. Sequential deceleration: -0.2% (FY24) -> +0.7% (Q1) -> -4.6% (Q2) -> -3.4% (Q3). Net sales for 9M FY25 are BELOW 9M FY24 in dollars ($887.7M vs $894.4M) — first sustained YoY decline since pandemic snap. Gross margin partially offset (37.3% 9M FY25 vs 35.7% 9M FY24) via packaging cost relief.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: FY2024 10-K framed Power+Brands volume softness as a small isolated -0.2%. Reality through Q3 FY25 (most recent pre-cutoff data point) is a clear and broadening volume decline, now impacting both Power+Brands and CSDs (Q2 FY25). Management is not lying — quarterly disclosures are explicit — but the FY24 risk-factor framing of competitive pressure was understated relative to what subsequent quarters revealed. Marketing spend also DECREASED in Q3 FY25 despite volume declines (per MD&A), which is the wrong response for a brand-driven business.

rfm_tuples.R: Nick A. Caporella (1) 88 Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer... Joseph G. Caporella (2) 63 President... George R. Bracken (3) 78 Executive Vice President Finance.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode B — derive succession/key-person risk. CEO age 88, EVP-Finance 78, President 63 (CEO's son). Verify governance independence, succession plan disclosure, controlled-company status.

The 10-K and DEF 14A do not flag controlled-company governance status, succession plan, or contingency for incapacity of the 88-year-old CEO whose privately-held company (CMA) provides senior corporate, financial, and executive functions. Joseph Caporella (son) is President; if Nick incapacitates, the controlled-company structure means succession is the family's call, not the public shareholders'.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B catch. Key-person risk at 88 is acute. Public-float governance protections are weak: 73.2% controller, financial-reporting outsourced to controller's wholly-owned management co (CMA), no succession disclosure, no audit-committee-driven CEO/CFO independence. Filing discloses individual facts (age, ownership %) but does NOT frame the cluster as a risk factor. Standard practice for an 88-year-old founder-CEO would be explicit succession-plan disclosure.

Hathorn (director) gifted 28,000 sh in Jan 2025 (tx_code='G'). NO Caporella sales (Nick or Joseph). NO Bracken open-market sales. Timing: sells cluster in early July 2024 (immediately AFTER the MW-disclosing 10-K + special dividend), and into Q3-Q4 FY2025 volume declines.

Independent directors (Conlee, Sheridan) ARE selling persistently into a declining share price, including immediately post-MW disclosure and into volume deceleration. Pattern is consistent with directors reducing exposure ahead of/during deteriorating fundamentals. Not a SEVERE flag (no executive insider selling, no 10b5-1 plan terminations disclosed), but the independent-director outflow during a governance/control-weakness/volume-decline window is a soft negative.

rfm_tuples.R: Implied claim — for a 73%-controlled company whose Chairman's wholly-owned management co (CMA) runs financial reporting, the disclosure should call out controlled-company status under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5615(c).
rfm_tuples.f: self_text — search 10-K and DEF 14A for explicit 'controlled company' language and Nasdaq 5615(c) election.
rfm_tuples.M_value: Neither the FY2024 10-K nor the August 2024 DEF 14A contains the phrase 'controlled company' or references Nasdaq Listing Rule 5615(c). The 10-K does not list controlling-shareholder concentration as a discrete risk factor (it is implicit from the executive officer table and DEF 14A ownership table). Nasdaq controlled-company exemptions (majority independent board, independent comp committee, independent nominating) are not explicitly elected or disclosed.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode B catch. A 73%-owned issuer is a textbook 'controlled company' under Nasdaq Rule 5615(c), eligible for exemption from majority-independent-board, independent-compensation-committee, and independent-nominating-committee requirements. The filings do not frame this as a status, even though the practical governance reality (Chairman's CMA running financial functions; son as President; 18-year audit relationship just terminated; multi-period material weakness) is exactly what those independent-committee rules are meant to mitigate. Honest by omission, not by commission.

summary: FIZZ is a structurally controlled (73.2% Caporella) defensive beverage company with a no-debt, cash-rich balance sheet that nonetheless shows an unusual cluster of governance/control flags for a 'boring middle' name. The FY2024 10-K discloses a multi-period material weakness in cash-flow statement controls (Q2 FY23 through Q3 FY24 — seven prior periods, all previously self-certified as effective), with the controls failure located precisely in the financial-reporting function that is outsourced to the 88-year-old Chairman's wholly-owned management company CMA ($11.9M FY24 fee, 1% of sales, uncapped). Four months later, 18-year auditor RSM US LLP was dismissed mid-fiscal-year, replaced by Grant Thornton, with the company asserting no Item 304 disagreements. Just before the 10-K filing, the board declared a $304M special cash dividend (the third ~$280-304M dividend in 4 years; cumulatively $864M extracted to shareholders, ~74% to the controlling Caporella family). Through pre-cutoff 10-Qs, volume trends have decelerated meaningfully (FY24 -0.2% -> Q2 FY25 -4.6% -> Q3 FY25 -3.4%), now impacting both Power+Brands and CSDs, while marketing spend was cut in Q3 FY25. Independent directors (Conlee, Sheridan) have been selling into the decline; the Caporellas have not. None of this is fraud — disclosure is technically present — but the cluster (controlled-company status not framed, succession risk at 88 not disclosed, financial-reporting outsourced to a controller-owned entity, MW where outsourced function is weakest, 18-year auditor terminated immediately post-MW, large pre-disclosure dividend, accelerating volume softness) is a classic 'Mode B' forensic profile that the FY24 10-K Risk Factors do not synthesize.
